newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees slight debt impact from U.S. rate rise.
newsitem.headline: China sees slight debt impact from U.S. rate rise.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve's quarter-point rate rise is expected to have limited impact on China's repayment of existing foreign debt, but could affect future debt offers, officials said on Wednesday.
"There will be no immediate impact," an official of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) said.
"We can't see any big impact," said an official of the People's Bank of China, the central bank.
The U.S. Federal Reserve's move on Tuesday, the first increase in over two years, pushed the key Fed funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight funds to 5.50 percent.
The Fed left the discount rate it charges banks for money unchanged at 5.0 percent.
The Federal Reserve said it was trying to stay a step ahead of inflation and keep economic expansion on track.
China's foreign debt reached $116.28 billion at the end of 1996, up by about 9.0 percent compared with a year ago.
The SAFE official said most of the foreign debt had fixed interest but a smaller portion had floating rates and would be affected. She did not give further details.
"This will affect future issues of debt in the U.S. market, however," she said.
China plans to issue 248.596 billion yuan ($29.95 billion) worth of domestic and foreign debt in 1997, up 27.3 percent from last year. It has not said how much foreign debt would be offered.
A total of 195.908 billion yuan would be needed to service domestic and foreign debt this year, the finance ministry has said.
